title: Where it grows
subtitle: Champagne and Germany
objectives: Explain why it suits cool, frosty places

steps.title: Champagne
steps.body: Meunier is about 30% of Champagne's vineyards, mainly in the Vallée de la Marne, where clay soils and frost-prone valleys suit it. It's also grown in the Aisne and the Aube. Outside Champagne, it's found in England, Germany, Australia's Great Western and California, mostly for sparkling wine.

steps.title: Frost and cold
steps.body: Meunier buds late, after the main spring frost risk, and ripens early. On cold, clay soils and in frost pockets, where Chardonnay and Pinot Noir struggle, Meunier gives reliable crops. That's why growers in the Marne valley rely on it.

steps.prompt: Why does Meunier suit Champagne's Vallée de la Marne?
steps.explanation: Late budding avoids spring frost in the valley's cold pockets.

steps.title: Germany
steps.body: In Germany, Meunier is called Schwarzriesling, black Riesling, or Müllerrebe, though it's unrelated to Riesling. It's grown mainly in Württemberg, for light reds and rosés. Some German producers also make sparkling Sekt with it.

steps.prompt: Match each name to its meaning or place.
steps.explanation: Meunier has names and homes in France and Germany.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Meunier is about 30% of Champagne, mainly in the Marne
It buds late and ripens early, avoiding frost
In Germany it's Schwarzriesling, grown in Württemberg
